summary:
Comunitat Valenciana stands under two layers of law. The national layer is Ley 4/2023, published in the Boletín Oficial del Estado on 28 February 2023, which establishes real and effective equality for trans persons and guarantees LGTBI rights: under Article 43 any person aged 16 or over may request rectification of the gender mention on their own civil registry entry directly before the Civil Registry, an administrative self-identification route that replaced the former requirement of a gender-dysphoria diagnosis plus two years of medical treatment. Recognition is possible from age 12 under conditions, and the law regulates consent for medical procedures on minors aged 12 to 16.

Other operative provisions of the same national statute include a ban on non-consensual normalising surgeries on intersex children, expanded assisted reproduction rules, parental recognition for unmarried same-sex couples, strengthened sexuality education, and anti-discrimination measures covering healthcare, employment and housing. Same-sex marriage and full adoption rights have been in force across Spain since 2005, and legal gender change does not require surgery or sterilisation.

Access to sex-separated facilities rests on legal gender self-determination rather than on biological sex, so the gender marker recorded in the civil registry is the operative basis for facility rules in Spain.

There is no free-standing criminal offence of gender-expression-based hate crime: the phrase 'gender expression' appears in no article of the Spanish Criminal Code. The hate-speech aggravating circumstance in Article 22.4 and the penalties of Article 510, one to four years' imprisonment plus a fine of six to twelve months, derive from Organic Law 6/2022, while Ley 4/2023 itself reformed offences against sexual freedom, including Articles 132, 173, 178 to 181 and 189 bis.

Enforcement of the gender-identity aggravation is documented. In July 2026 the Tribunal de Instancia in Vigo applied the transfobia aggravating circumstance for the first time in a misdemeanour case concerning threats sent by WhatsApp to a trans woman, fining the author EUR 300. Within the Comunitat Valenciana, the Audiencia Provincial de Valencia, Section 5, sentenced a group over a June 2022 incident in a park in the Patraix district of Valencia, where an 18-year-old and several minors insulted, chased, filmed and mocked a trans woman because of her gender identity; the adult defendant accepted six months' prison, suspended on condition of committing no offence for two years, plus a EUR 720 fine and a EUR 1,000 moral-damages payment to the victim, and two minors were sentenced separately to supervision measures. The case was handled by the hate-crime prosecutor.

The regional layer adds two statutes of its own. Ley 8/2017, de 7 de abril, integral del reconocimiento del derecho a la identidad y a la expresión de género, published as BOE-A-2017-5118, makes its purpose the guarantee of an adequate normative framework for gender self-determination for people whose felt gender identity differs from the one assigned at birth; it obliges public bodies of the Comunitat Valenciana to treat people according to their felt gender identity, and its Title III provides for administrative documentation and an advice-and-support service for trans people and their families. Ley 23/2018, de 29 de noviembre, de igualdad de las personas LGTBI, published as BOE-A-2019-281, is the community's general equality statute: it covers non-discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity or expression, sets access and admission rights under Article 56, reverses the burden of proof under Article 57, and establishes a Title V regime of administrative infringements and sanctions under Articles 58 to 66 for discrimination against LGTBI people.

With administrative self-declaration at national level, Spain stands alongside Argentina, Ireland, Portugal and Uruguay.
tangentialFactors:
The Comunitat Valenciana is one of a minority of autonomous communities carrying a trans-specific statute as well as a general LGTBI statute. The Spanish trans-rights platform Plataforma Trans lists the community with two statutes, Ley 8/2017 and Ley 23/2018, while other communities in the same inventory carry a single statute, among them Cataluña with Ley 11/2014 and Aragón with Ley 4/2018.

A 2025 radiography of public educational policies published by the Spanish LGTBI federation places Comunitat Valenciana with Madrid, Extremadura, Murcia and Navarra among the leaders on educational policy coverage, and records that the Valencian parliament completed its gender legislation. The radiography covers gender-identity protocols and education legislation in each autonomous community.

Access to sex-separated facilities in Spain rests on legal gender self-determination rather than on biological sex, in contrast to the stricter single-sex-space approach being adopted in the United Kingdom on biological-sex lines, with restrictions applied case by case rather than as a blanket ban.

Spain's administrative self-declaration regime is comparatively unusual: a 2016 survey of 23 countries ranked Spain the most trans-supportive of the group surveyed and the only country where a majority supported unrestricted legal gender designation change. That ranking is a dated baseline predating Ley 4/2023.
localsOnly:
Residents of the Comunitat Valenciana can invoke two regional statutes directly. Ley 8/2017 requires public bodies of the community to treat people according to their felt gender identity, and its Title III provides administrative documentation procedures together with an advice-and-support service for trans people and their families. Ley 23/2018 supplies the enforcement machinery for complaints: Article 56 governs access and admission, Article 57 reverses the burden of proof in discrimination proceedings, and Title V, Articles 58 to 66, sets out administrative infringements and sanctions for discrimination against LGTBI people.

The Patraix case shows the hate-crime channel working in practice at provincial level. The Audiencia Provincial de Valencia, Section 5, handled the June 2022 incident; the adult defendant received six months' prison suspended for a two-year good-conduct period, a EUR 720 fine and a EUR 1,000 moral-damages indemnity to the victim, while the two minors were sentenced separately to supervision measures. The prosecution was conducted by the fiscal coordinadora de delitos de odio, the hate-crime coordinating prosecutor.

The national statute's resident-facing provisions extend to intersex children, whose non-consensual normalising surgeries are banned, to unmarried same-sex couples, who gain parental recognition, and to sexuality education, which is strengthened, alongside anti-discrimination measures in healthcare, employment and housing. Consent for medical procedures on minors aged 12 to 16 is regulated by the same law.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory addresses how the Comunitat Valenciana's two regional statutes interact with a visitor's foreign civil-registry entry. Whether the Article 43 route before the Civil Registry is available to a non-resident, and what documents a foreign trans visitor would need to present, is unresolved here.

The July 2026 transfobia aggravating-circumstance decision was rendered by the Tribunal de Instancia in Vigo, which lies outside the Comunitat Valenciana; no equivalent first-instance decision from within the community is sourced, so the regional enforcement record rests on the single Audiencia Provincial de Valencia sentence.

Nothing in the inventory reports on regional statistics for hate-crime reporting, on waiting times for gender-marker rectification before the Civil Registry in this community, or on the practical operation of the Title III advice-and-support service. Regional data on detention or prison placement for trans detainees is likewise not sourced.

The 2016 23-country survey ranking predates Ley 4/2023 by seven years and should not be read as a current measure.
